doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
title: Motivic development and the twelve-tone Point Blank score
summary: Mandel explains that he wrote Point Blank (1967) around a tone row and motif, as one of his favorite film projects.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Yeah, there are some film scores of his that maybe we should – there’s a technique he uses in his, some of his film scores like for, Three Days of the Condor…
Where he does, I guess what you’d call motivic development…
Just starting out with a basic motif and developing it throughout the film.
Is that a technique that interests you in doing scores?
Sure, I’ve done that, Point Blank’s a good example of something I did in, fact I wrote that whole – That’s totally a twelve tone score, I wrote it around a row and a motif, a tone-row and a motif.
When did that come out, I’m not familiar with that one?
1967. That was one of my favorite projects.
Does that show up on television or anything anymore?
Oh yeah, all over the place, Lee Marvin, Angie Dickinson, a lot of good actors in there.
I’ll have to watch for that.
Lloyd Bochner, a real solid bunch of Canadian actors, John Vernon. John Boorman film. A lot of fun to do that movie, work, but fun, that’s one of the more rewarding ones.
